shortExplanation: The average rises from eighty-six to eighty-seven, an increase of one.
detailedSteps: The first three scores sum to $87+83+88=258$, so their average is $258/3=86$.
Including the fourth score gives total $258+90=348$ and average $348/4=87$. The increase is $87-86=1$.
keyIdeas: Compare the two actual averages
commonMistakes: Dividing both totals by the same number of examinations.
difficultyNotes: The denominator changes when a new observation is included.

shortExplanation: Two successive squarings give $\sqrt{x}=7$ and $x=49$.
detailedSteps: The actual equation is $\sqrt{2+\sqrt{x}}=3$. Squaring gives $2+\sqrt{x}=9$, hence $\sqrt{x}=7$.
Squaring once more gives $x=49$. Substitution verifies $\sqrt{2+\sqrt{49}}=\sqrt9=3$; both radicals use their nonnegative values.
keyIdeas: Undo the outer square root before the inner one
commonMistakes: Squaring the inner radical before isolating it.
difficultyNotes: Keep the order of the two radical operations explicit.

shortExplanation: The advertisement totals $9992$ cents, seven cents less than the store price.
detailedSteps: The three payments cost $3\cdot2998=8994$ cents. Add the one-time shipping charge of $998$ cents to get $9992$ cents.
The store price is $9999$ cents, so the saving is $9999-9992=7$ cents. The shipping charge is paid once.
keyIdeas: Work in integer cents
commonMistakes: Adding the one-time shipping charge to each payment.
difficultyNotes: Integer cents avoid rounding artifacts in currency subtraction.

detailedSteps: Combine the first two percentage relations: $M=0.3Q=0.3(0.2P)=0.06P$. The third gives $N=0.5P$.
The requested quotient is defined only when $N\ne0$, so the common factor $P$ is nonzero and cancels: $M/N=0.06/0.5=3/25$.
keyIdeas: Express both quantities in the same base
commonMistakes: Adding successive percentage factors instead of multiplying them.
difficultyNotes: A common reference quantity makes chained percentages easy to compare.

shortExplanation: The density estimate gives $51.84$ million ants, closest to fifty million.
detailedSteps: The field area is $300\cdot400=120000$ square feet. Each square foot contains $12^2=144$ square inches.
The estimated count is $120000\cdot144\cdot3=51840000$. Among the five actual choices, fifty million is the closest approximation. This is an estimate from sampling, not an exact census.
keyIdeas: Square the length conversion when converting area
commonMistakes: Multiplying the area by twelve instead of one hundred forty-four.
difficultyNotes: Area units require the square of the linear conversion.

shortExplanation: The folded normal of face $C$ is opposite the normal of $x$.
detailedSteps: Use the exact source net: $A$ is to the right of $x$, $B$ above $A$, $C$ to the right of $B$, $D$ above $C$, and $E$ to the right of $D$. Start with $x$ facing upward.
For a consistent fold, these six faces have outward normals $+z,+x,+y,-z,-x,-y$, respectively, in that order. Each fold is a quarter-turn about its shared edge.
Thus $C$ faces $-z$ while $x$ faces $+z$. They are the opposite faces. Reversing the fold convention reflects the entire cube and preserves the same opposite pairs.
keyIdeas: Track the directions of all folded face normals
commonMistakes: Reading which net squares are far apart without actually folding the intervening edges.
difficultyNotes: The actual stepped net, rather than a memorized generic net, determines the pair.

shortExplanation: The flight time is $16\pi\approx50.27$ hours, nearest to fifty.
detailedSteps: At negligible altitude the route length is the equatorial circumference $2\pi\cdot4000=8000\pi$ miles.
The given speed is relative to Earth, so the time is $8000\pi/500=16\pi\approx50.27$ hours. The closest listed estimate is fifty hours.
keyIdeas: Divide the equatorial circumference by the stated speed
commonMistakes: Using the diameter instead of the circumference.
difficultyNotes: The stated reference frame already supplies the relevant speed.

shortExplanation: The scale factor is $DE/AC=2/3$, so $BD=(2/3)AB=20/3$.
detailedSteps: Pythagoras gives $AB=\sqrt{6^2+8^2}=10$. Because $DE$ and $AC$ are both perpendicular to $BC$, they are parallel.
Triangles $BDE$ and $BAC$ share the angle at $B$ and have right angles at $E$ and $C$, so they are similar. Therefore $BD/AB=DE/AC=4/6=2/3$.
The required length is $BD=(2/3)\cdot10=20/3$. The corresponding $BE=16/3$ lies within the original side of length eight.
keyIdeas: Use the similar right triangles with the shared angle at B
commonMistakes: Matching the hypotenuse to a leg when writing the similarity ratio.
difficultyNotes: The explicit right angle determines the parallel sides.

shortExplanation: There are eight small triangles, four middle-sized triangles and four half-square triangles, for sixteen.
detailedSteps: Scale the square to side two. Its four corners, four side midpoints and central intersection are the only possible triangle vertices formed by the drawn straight lines.
The eight wedges from the center to neighboring boundary vertices have area $1/2$. Four triangles use an entire square side as base and the center as apex; each has area one.

Each selection of three square corners gives a triangle of area two, producing four more. No other vertex triples have all three sides on the drawn segments; checking those segments completes the classification.
The total is $8+4+4=16$. Larger triangles remain eligible even when internal lines subdivide them.
keyIdeas: Count triangles by their area scale in the actual drawing
commonMistakes: Counting only the eight smallest regions.
difficultyNotes: Classification by scale prevents both omissions and double counting.

shortExplanation: The vertices are $(0,0),(-6,6),(6,6)$, so the area is thirty-six.
detailedSteps: The two sloping lines meet at $(0,0)$. Intersecting each with $y=6$ gives $(6,6)$ and $(-6,6)$.
The horizontal base has length twelve and its perpendicular height from the origin is six. Thus the area is $\tfrac12\cdot12\cdot6=36$.
keyIdeas: Find the three pairwise line intersections
commonMistakes: Using the sloping side length as the height above the horizontal base.
difficultyNotes: The horizontal line makes the base-height calculation direct.

shortExplanation: There are two leading digits, six middle pairs and two final digits, giving twenty-four.
detailedSteps: The interval restricts the thousands digit to four or five. Divisibility by five restricts the units digit to zero or five.
The two middle digits satisfy $3\le b<c\le6$. Choosing two of the four digits $3,4,5,6$ determines their increasing order, giving $\binom42=6$ pairs.
These three independent choices produce $2\cdot6\cdot2=24$ distinct numbers; every resulting number meets the original interval condition.
keyIdeas: Choose the leading digit, the ordered middle pair and the last digit
commonMistakes: Counting both orders of the middle digits despite the strict inequality.
difficultyNotes: Every digit restriction controls a separate choice.

shortExplanation: The slope must be both nonnegative and nonpositive, so the function is constantly five.
detailedSteps: Write $f(x)=mx+b$. The inequality $f(1)\le f(2)$ gives $m\ge0$, while $f(3)\ge f(4)$ gives $m\le0$. Hence $m=0$.
The function is constant. Since $f(5)=5$, that constant is five, so $f(0)=5$.
keyIdeas: Read the inequalities as opposite restrictions on the slope
commonMistakes: Assuming one inequality makes the slope strictly positive.
difficultyNotes: Nonstrict inequalities permit, and here force, a constant function.

shortExplanation: Replacing every two by six corrects the addition, so $d+e=2+6=8$.
detailedSteps: The displayed addition has error $742586+829430-1212016=360000$. Replacing digit $d$ by $e$ changes this error by $(e-d)K_d$, where $K_d$ is the net sum of its place values in the two addends minus those in the result.

Since $|e-d|\le9$, only digits with $|K_d|\ge40000$ can repair that error. From the actual display these are $d=1,2,7,8$, with weights $-1010010,-90000,100000,100010$, respectively. None of the first, third or fourth weights divides $360000$, so only $d=2$ is possible.

Then $360000-90000(e-2)=0$ gives $e=6$. The corrected equality is $746586+869430=1616016$, and the requested sum is eight. All replaced digits, including both occurrences in the result, have been included.
keyIdeas: Measure how one digit replacement changes the addition error
commonMistakes: Changing just one occurrence of a digit when the instruction applies to every occurrence.
difficultyNotes: The column positions supply a short completeness argument.

shortExplanation: The only term that changes sign is $x$, so $f(3)=f(-3)+6=8$.
detailedSteps: The terms $ax^4$ and $-bx^2$, as well as the constant five, have the same values at three and negative three.
Therefore $f(3)-f(-3)=3-(-3)=6$. With $f(-3)=2$, the requested value is eight; finding either coefficient separately is unnecessary.
keyIdeas: Cancel the even-power terms at opposite inputs
commonMistakes: Trying to solve two coefficients from one supplied equation.
difficultyNotes: Symmetry isolates the requested value without recovering the whole function.

shortExplanation: The bug follows $5\to1\to2\to4\to1$, so jump $1995$ ends at four.
detailedSteps: The actual clockwise rule sends five to one, one to two, two to four, and four back to one. After the first jump the cycle is $1,2,4$, repeating every three jumps.
Jump numbers congruent to one, two and zero modulo three end at one, two and four, respectively. Since $1995$ is divisible by three, the final point is four.
keyIdeas: Separate the first jump from the repeating three-state cycle
commonMistakes: Including the starting point five as a recurring state of the cycle.
difficultyNotes: A short transient can matter when indexing a periodic walk.

shortExplanation: The maximum difference is about $21666.7$, rounding to twenty-two thousand.
detailedSteps: Atlanta attendance lies between $0.9\cdot50000=45000$ and $1.1\cdot50000=55000$. Boston instead satisfies $0.9B\le60000\le1.1B$, so $60000/1.1\le B\le60000/0.9$.
The greatest difference occurs with Boston at its upper bound and Atlanta at its lower bound: $60000/0.9-45000=65000/3\approx21666.7$. The opposite direction gives only $55000-60000/1.1\approx454.5$.

Attendance is integer-valued: Boston can have $66666$ fans and Atlanta $45000$, attaining difference $21666$ under both actual percentage conditions. Either the integer maximum or its continuous bound rounds to $22000$ to the nearest thousand.
keyIdeas: Use the correct reference quantity in each percentage bound
commonMistakes: Treating both ten-percent conditions as percentages of the quoted estimates.
difficultyNotes: The wording changes the percentage denominator between the two games.

shortExplanation: The angle between tangent $AB$ and chord $AD$ is seventy-two degrees, giving minor arc measure $144^\circ$.
detailedSteps: Each regular-pentagon interior angle is $108^\circ$. Triangle $AED$ is isosceles with angle $AED=108^\circ$, so its base angle $EAD$ is $36^\circ$.
Thus $\angle DAB=108^\circ-36^\circ=72^\circ$. Because $AB$ is tangent to the circle at $A$, the tangent-chord theorem makes the intercepted arc $AD$ twice that angle: $144^\circ$.
This is less than $180^\circ$, so it is the requested minor arc. The supplied tangency at $D$ is consistent with the same circle, as the independent center construction verifies.
keyIdeas: Apply the tangent-chord theorem after finding the pentagon angle
commonMistakes: Using the pentagon side arc instead of the arc on the different tangent circle.
difficultyNotes: The circle need not be the pentagon circumcircle.

shortExplanation: $OB\sin30^\circ\le AB=1$ gives $OB\le2$, and equality is attainable.
detailedSteps: Let $OA=a$ and $OB=b$. The cosine rule rearranges to $AB^2=(a-b\cos30^\circ)^2+b^2\sin^230^\circ$. Its first term is nonnegative, so $1\ge b^2/4$, yielding $b\le2$.
Equality occurs at $b=2$ and $a=b\cos30^\circ=\sqrt3$. Both points lie on their required positive rays and their separation is one. Hence the bound is the maximum.
keyIdeas: Bound the perpendicular distance from B to the other ray
commonMistakes: Giving a bound without checking it can be attained on the rays.
difficultyNotes: The perpendicular projection provides both the bound and its equality case.

shortExplanation: The inner side is $1/\sqrt3$ times the outer side, so the area ratio is one third.
detailedSteps: Scale the outer side to one, with $B=(0,0)$, $C=(1,0)$ and $A=(1/2,\sqrt3/2)$. Write $D=(t,0)$. Since $DE$ is vertical and $E$ lies on $AC$, its height is $h=\sqrt3(1-t)$.

The third vertex of the inner equilateral triangle on the depicted left side is $F=(t-\sqrt3h/2,h/2)$. Its membership on $AB$, whose equation is $y=\sqrt3x$, gives $h/2=\sqrt3(t-\sqrt3h/2)$, or $2h=\sqrt3t$.
Combining the height equations gives $t=2/3$ and $h=1/\sqrt3$. Thus the inner-to-outer side ratio is $1/\sqrt3$ and the area ratio is its square, $1/3$. All vertices belong to the actual sides shown.
keyIdeas: Determine the unique inscribed coordinates before comparing areas
commonMistakes: Using a side-length ratio directly as the area ratio.
difficultyNotes: The explicit perpendicular side fixes the otherwise variable rotation.

shortExplanation: The two even-sum cases contribute $27/125$ and $32/125$, totaling $59/125$.
detailedSteps: Use the customary independent uniform draws with replacement. Three of the five entries are odd, so $ab$ is odd with probability $(3/5)^2=9/25$ and even with probability $16/25$.
The sum $ab+c$ is even exactly when both terms have the same parity. Its probability is $(9/25)(3/5)+(16/25)(2/5)=59/125$. The two cases are disjoint and exhaust the event.
keyIdeas: Match the parity of the product with the parity of the last draw
commonMistakes: Treating the product as equally likely to be odd or even.
difficultyNotes: Replacement uses the standard independent sampling model; the convention is stated explicitly.

shortExplanation: The circle $x^2+y^2=25$ supplies five other antipodal lattice pairs, hence five rectangles.
detailedSteps: The given opposite vertices have midpoint $(0,0)$ and distance five from that midpoint. Every other rectangle vertex lies on the circle $x^2+y^2=25$, by the right-angle diameter theorem, and its opposite vertex is its negative.
The integer points on that circle are $(\pm5,0),(0,\pm5),(\pm4,\pm3),(\pm3,\pm4)$, twelve in total. The given pair removes two, leaving ten available vertices.
Each pair $P,-P$ describes the same nondegenerate rectangle, so there are $10/2=5$ rectangles. Every remaining pair is distinct from the given diagonal endpoints and realizes a right-angle rectangle.
keyIdeas: Use the circle determined by the fixed rectangle diagonal
commonMistakes: Counting each rectangle twice by distinguishing its two remaining opposite vertices.
difficultyNotes: The fixed diagonal determines one circle even when the rectangle is rotated.

shortExplanation: The cut removes a right triangle of legs twelve and five from a $31$ by $25$ rectangle, leaving $745$.
detailedSteps: Let $W,H$ be the untouched rectangle sides and $w,h$ the shortened sides after the corner is cut. They satisfy $W>w$, $H>h$, and the fifth side is the slant length $s$, with $s^2=(W-w)^2+(H-h)^2$.

For any proposed $s$, the other four lengths can be paired in three ways. The greatest possible sum of squared differences for $s=19,20,25,31$ is respectively $349,360,325,145$, each smaller than its required square. Thus none can be the slant side.
For $s=13$, the three sums are $37,157,169$; only $169=13^2$ works. Its two differences are $31-19=12$ and $25-20=5$, determining the rectangle dimensions up to interchange.
The remaining area is $31\cdot25-\tfrac12\cdot12\cdot5=775-30=745$. This assignment produces a valid positive cut at one corner, so it is attainable.
keyIdeas: Try the five possible cut-side roles rather than their numerical order
commonMistakes: Assuming the largest listed side must be the cut slant.
difficultyNotes: The boundary order is unknown; the right-triangle relation determines it.

shortExplanation: The allowable obtuse values are $5$ through $10$ and $19$ through $25$, thirteen in total.
detailedSteps: The strict triangle inequalities require $|15-11|<k<15+11$, hence integer values $5\le k\le25$.
For $k\le15$, the longest side is fifteen. Obtuseness requires $15^2>11^2+k^2$, or $k^2<104$, giving $k=5,6,7,8,9,10$.
For $k>15$, the longest side is $k$. Now obtuseness requires $k^2>11^2+15^2=346$, giving $k=19,20,\ldots,25$. The two ranges contain six and seven values, totaling thirteen.
keyIdeas: Separate the two possible longest-side cases
commonMistakes: Applying the same largest-side inequality after k exceeds fifteen.
difficultyNotes: Both the triangle inequality and the obtuse inequality are strict.

shortExplanation: The primitive positive triple is $(A,B,C)=(2,3,1)$, so the sum is six.
detailedSteps: Combining and exponentiating the base-two-hundred logarithms gives $5^A2^B=200^C$. Since $200=2^3\cdot5^2$, unique prime factorization requires $A=2C$ and $B=3C$.
The greatest common divisor of $2C,3C,C$ is $C$. The stated absence of a common factor greater than one forces $C=1$, and then $A=2$, $B=3$. Their sum is six.
keyIdeas: Compare prime exponents after exponentiating the logarithm equation
commonMistakes: Requiring pairwise coprimality instead of the stated common-factor condition for all three.
difficultyNotes: Prime factorization proves the integer relation uniquely.

shortExplanation: The second-largest entry can be $10,12,14,16,18$ or $20$, giving six possibilities.
detailedSteps: Order the five entries as $a\le b\le8\le d\le e$. Their total is sixty, and range eighteen gives $e=a+18$. The stated mode eight must occur at least twice.

If $d=8$, then the median and fourth entry are both eight. The sum equation becomes $2a+b=26$, impossible because $a,b\le8$ makes its left side at most twenty-four. Thus the repeated eight must be $b=8$.
Now $a+8+8+d+(a+18)=60$ yields $d=26-2a$. The conditions $d\ge8$ and $d\le a+18$ give $3\le a\le8$. For these six integer values, $d$ is $20,18,16,14,12,10$, respectively.

Each corresponding list has mean twelve, range eighteen, median eight and eight as its unique most frequent value. Thus every candidate occurs and there are exactly six distinct second-largest values.
keyIdeas: Use the repeated median and the total before counting values
commonMistakes: Counting different lists when the question asks different values of one order statistic.
difficultyNotes: The ordinary mode convention means a repeated most frequent value; every constructed list has a unique mode.

shortExplanation: The two identities are $r^2+OE^2=36$ and $r^2-OE^2=12$, giving $r^2=24$.
detailedSteps: Let the radius be $r$ and put $x=OE$. The perpendicular diameters make triangle $DOE$ right, so $r^2+x^2=DE^2=36$.
At the internal chord intersection $E$, the intersecting-chords theorem gives $EA\cdot EB=DE\cdot EF=6\cdot2=12$. Along diameter $AB$, this is $(r+x)(r-x)=r^2-x^2$.
Adding the two equations yields $2r^2=48$, so $r^2=24$ and the circle area is $24\pi$. The resulting $x^2=12<r^2$ also verifies the internal intersection.
keyIdeas: Combine the right triangle with intersecting chords
commonMistakes: Using the full chord length eight as one factor of the intersecting-chords product.
difficultyNotes: The sum and difference of squares eliminate the unknown offset.

shortExplanation: The row sums satisfy $f(n)=2f(n-1)+2$, giving $f(100)=2^{100}-2\equiv74\pmod{100}$.
detailedSteps: Row $n$ has boundary values $n-1$. When the preceding row is summed into adjacent pairs, its interior entries are counted twice and its two boundary entries once. Adding the new boundaries therefore gives $f(n)=2f(n-1)-2(n-2)+2(n-1)=2f(n-1)+2$. The formula also checks directly for row two.
Since $f(1)=0$, the shifted sum $f(n)+2$ doubles at every step. Thus $f(n)=2^n-2$.
Modulo one hundred, $2^{20}\equiv76$, and $76^2\equiv76$. Consequently $2^{100}=(2^{20})^5\equiv76$, so the required remainder is $76-2=74$.
keyIdeas: Sum the interior recurrence and keep the boundary correction
commonMistakes: Doubling the whole preceding row without correcting how its boundary entries are counted.
difficultyNotes: The boundary correction changes the usual Pascal-triangle row sum.

shortExplanation: The middle half-chord has square $46$, so its full length has square $184$.
detailedSteps: Put the two chords at signed offsets $m-3$ and $m+3$ from the center, since their separation is six. Their half-length squares are $25$ and $49$, each equal to the radius square minus its corresponding offset square.
Averaging gives $(25+49)/2=r^2-m^2-9$. Thus the middle half-chord square is $r^2-m^2=37+9=46$.
The full middle length is twice its half-length, so its square is $4\cdot46=184$. The signed-offset calculation works whether the original chords straddle the center or lie on the same side.
keyIdeas: Average the half-chord squares and correct for the midpoint offset
commonMistakes: Averaging the chord lengths directly instead of their squared half-lengths.
difficultyNotes: The midpoint correction follows from a quadratic, not linear, chord-length relation.

shortExplanation: There are $3^5-3$ ordered distinct triples; dividing by six gives forty sets.
detailedSteps: The product is $2310=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11$, with five different primes. Assigning each prime to one of three labelled factors gives $3^5=243$ ordered positive triples, with an empty box representing the factor one.

Two factors could be equal only if both equal one: any prime common to equal factors would occur twice in the squarefree product. The repeated-factor triples are therefore precisely the three permutations of $(1,1,2310)$.
Remove these three triples. Each remaining triple has three distinct entries and exactly $3!=6$ orders representing the same three-element set. Thus the count is $(243-3)/6=40$.
keyIdeas: Distribute the five distinct prime factors into three labelled boxes
commonMistakes: Dividing all ordered triples by six before removing triples with repeated entries.
difficultyNotes: Squarefreeness makes the only repeated-entry exception easy to classify.

shortExplanation: The plane is $x+y+z=9/2$ and meets the six, seven and six cubes in index-sum layers two, three and four.
detailedSteps: Place the large cube at $[0,3]^3$ and choose its diagonal from $(0,0,0)$ to $(3,3,3)$. A plane perpendicular to that diagonal through its midpoint has equation $x+y+z=9/2$. Other body diagonals give equivalent counts by cube symmetry.

A unit cube with lower corner $(i,j,k)$, where each index is zero, one or two, has sum-coordinate interval $[i+j+k,i+j+k+3]$. The plane meets it exactly when its integer index sum is two, three or four. Equality with either endpoint of this sum-coordinate interval cannot occur because the plane level is a half-integer.

For sum two, the index types are $(2,0,0)$ and $(1,1,0)$, three orders each, giving six. For sum three there are six orders of $(2,1,0)$ and one $(1,1,1)$, giving seven. Sum four has six cubes by the reflection $(i,j,k)\mapsto(2-i,2-j,2-k)$.
The count is $6+7+6=19$. Every counted cube has an actual interior slice, so no convention about touching edges changes this count.
keyIdeas: Compare the plane level with each unit cube’s minimum and maximum
commonMistakes: Counting only the central index-sum layer instead of all cubes crossed by the plane.
difficultyNotes: A three-dimensional slice is easiest to count through coordinate intervals.
